checks.title: Most likely place
checks.detail: Found ${param.incident.service} carrying most of the window's requests, so looked there first.

checks.title: Mixed outcomes
checks.detail: Filtered to ${param.incident.service}: its requests returned HTTP ${param.incident.status} as well as 200.

checks.title: First failure

answer.evidence: Every failure ran ${param.incident.bad_version} while the successes ran ${param.incident.good_version} or ${param.incident.legacy_version}. Hosts and endpoints were mixed, so the version sets the failures apart.

scope.concept: The window has to reach back before the rollout. A fixed start stays put while you investigate; “the last 15 minutes” moves with the clock.
scope.narration: The new release began rolling out at ${incident.rollout_clock} (${incident.rollout_ago}). Start the window a little before then, so you can see the rollout and the traffic just before it.
scope.reasoning: Starting just before the rollout puts the old release's healthy traffic next to the new one's. A fixed start keeps both in view, however long you take.
scope.evidence: The histogram should start a little before the rollout.

demonstration.narration: The rollout began at ${incident.rollout_clock}. I'll start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}, the five-minute mark before it. A fixed start keeps the rollout in view, however long we take.
demonstration.evidence: The window now starts at ${incident.window_start_clock}, before the rollout at ${incident.rollout_clock}. The start is a fixed time, so the first requests on the new release can't slide out of view.

drifts.note: You started searching before setting the time window; this step is about choosing when to look.

hints: The briefing says when the rollout began; the window has to start before that. A fixed start stays put, where the last 15 minutes moves on with the clock.
Click the date box at the top of Discover and type a start date and time followed by “to now”.
Start the window at ${incident.window_start_clock}: type “${incident.window_start_typed} to now”. Show me can do it for you.

isolate.title: Look at the busiest service first
isolate.concept: A filter pill keeps only one value of a field, so you can look at that service on its own.
isolate.narration: Start with the most likely place. Filter service.name to the service with the most requests: in its Top values, click the + next to it. Then read the HTTP status codes in the results.
isolate.reasoning: Looking at one service on its own shows whether its requests are failing.
isolate.evidence: Only that service's requests remain, some failing and some succeeding.

demonstration.narration: I'll start with the most likely place: I'll filter service.name to the service with the most requests, then read their status codes.
demonstration.reasoning: The window mixes every service's traffic. A filter pill keeps only this service, so its status codes show whether its requests fail.
demonstration.evidence: Some ${param.incident.service} requests fail and others succeed: the http.response.status_code column shows both ${param.incident.status} and 200. The service.name: ${param.incident.service} filter pill keeps only this service's requests. Next, we keep only the failures.

hints: Start with the service that has the most requests: it's the most likely place for the failures.
Open service.name's Top values and click the + next to the service with the most requests. Then read the http.response.status_code column.
Filter service.name for ${param.incident.service} with the + in its Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: You filtered on the service ${action.value}; check that it's the service that stood out in service.name's Top values.

inspect.title: Look for what the failures share
inspect.concept: Field statistics counts the distinct values of every field at once. A field with one value across all the failures is something they share.
inspect.narration: Switch from Documents to Field statistics. It counts the distinct values of each column for the failures in view. Look for a column about what handled the request (host, endpoint or version) with one value across all of them.
inspect.reasoning: Any field could set the failures apart. Field statistics shows every field's distinct values at once, so you don't have to guess which one to check.
inspect.evidence: One field has a single value across every failed request.

demonstration.narration: I'll switch to Field statistics, which counts the distinct values of every field for the failures in view.
demonstration.reasoning: Any field could set the failures apart, so we scan them all instead of guessing one. The status code and message describe the failure itself, so they match on every failure anyway. Fields about what handled each request, like host.name, url.path and service.version, can show what the failures share.
demonstration.evidence: service.version has 1 distinct value: every failed request ran the same version. host.name and url.path have several, so the failures are spread across hosts and endpoints. The service.version column will show which version it is.

hints: Compare every field at once, rather than guessing which one matters.
Switch from Documents to Field statistics, above the results, and read the Distinct values column for host.name, url.path and service.version.
Open Field statistics and read service.version's distinct values; Show me can do it for you.
Sum up what the failed requests share, and when the first one happened.
Use the coach's answer form. Give what the failures share, the service, the time of the first failure as Discover shows it, and the comparison with the successes.
Submit what they share, the service, the first failure and the conclusion; Show me shows the reference summary.

goal.title: Look at which service the window is about
goal.concept: A field's Top values show which service has most of the window's traffic: the most likely place to look first.
goal.narration: The report doesn't name the failing service. Open the service.name field in the sidebar and read its Top values. The service with most of the window's requests is the most likely place to look first.
goal.reasoning: Filtering on a guessed service would assume the answer. The Top values show which service the incident window is about.
goal.evidence: The service.name Top values show one service carrying most of the window.

demonstration.narration: The report doesn't name the failing service. I'll check service.name Top values to see which service most of this window's requests belong to.
demonstration.reasoning: Filtering on a guessed service would assume the answer. Top values count every request in the window, so the next filter comes from the data.
demonstration.evidence: The highlighted row, ${param.incident.service}, has most of the window's requests, well ahead of the other services. That makes it the most likely place for the failures, so we'll look there first.

hints: Let the data show which service the incident window is about, instead of assuming one.
Open the service.name field in the sidebar and read its Top values (or add it as a column).
Open service.name and read its Top values; Show me can open the reference field.

drifts.note: You opened ${action.field}; this step is about which service the window is about.
You filtered before reading service.name's Top values, so the filter rests on a guess.

goal.title: Keep only the failed requests
goal.concept: To find what failed requests have in common, look at them on their own first.
goal.narration: Keep only this service's failed requests. Open the event.outcome field's Top values and click the + next to the value for failed requests.
goal.reasoning: With only the failures in view, anything they all share stands out. Successful requests mixed in would blur it.
goal.evidence: A filter pill keeps only the failed requests.

demonstration.narration: I'll keep only the failed requests, with the + next to failure in event.outcome's Top values.
demonstration.reasoning: To find what the failures have in common, we look at them on their own. Successful requests mixed in would blur any pattern.
demonstration.evidence: The event.outcome: failure filter pill keeps only the failed ${param.incident.service} requests, and the hit count shows how many. Next, we look for something they all share.

hints: Look at the failed requests on their own.
Open event.outcome's Top values and click the + next to the value for failed requests. (A range on http.response.status_code from 500 up works too.)
Filter event.outcome for failure with the + in its Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: That keeps the ${action.value} requests. This step looks at the failures on their own.

goal.title: Find when the first failure happened
goal.concept: Sorting oldest first puts the start of a change at the top of the table. Newest first hides it at the bottom.
goal.narration: Sort the results oldest first, and read the time of the first failure.
goal.reasoning: The brief asks when the first failure happened. Discover lists the newest requests first, so the first failure is at the far end. Sorting the other way brings it to the top.
goal.evidence: With only failures in view, the top row is the first failure.

demonstration.narration: I'll switch back to the documents and sort @timestamp oldest first, so the first failure comes to the top.
demonstration.reasoning: Discover lists the newest requests first, which puts the start of a problem at the bottom of a long list. Sorted oldest first, the first failure is the top row.
demonstration.evidence: The first failed request came at ${incident.first_clock}, on ${param.incident.bad_version} in the service.version column, shortly after the rollout began at ${incident.rollout_clock}. Next, we check whether any successful request ran that version.

hints: Discover lists the newest requests first; the first failure is at the other end.
Open the @timestamp column's header menu and choose Sort Old-New, then read the top row.
Sort @timestamp Old-New and read the first row's time; Show me can sort it for you.

drifts.note: That sorts newest first; the first appearance is at the oldest end.
You sorted by ${action.field}; the first appearance is about time, so sort @timestamp.

goal.title: Check the successful requests
goal.concept: Comparing failed requests with successful ones shows whether what the failed ones share really sets them apart.
goal.narration: Turn the event.outcome pill around: click it and choose Exclude results. Then read service.version on the successful requests.
goal.reasoning: Every failure ran one version. That explains them only if no successful request ran it too.
goal.evidence: The successful requests ran other versions.

demonstration.narration: I'll turn the event.outcome pill around, to see the successful requests instead.
demonstration.reasoning: Every failure ran the same version. That explains them only if the successful requests ran other versions. One pill switches between the two sides.
demonstration.evidence: Only successful requests remain, and in the service.version column they ran ${param.incident.good_version} or ${param.incident.legacy_version}, never ${param.incident.bad_version}. ${truth.conclusion}

hints: Check whether any successful request ran the same version as the failed ones.
Click the event.outcome pill to open its menu and choose Exclude results. Then read the service.version column.
Turn the event.outcome pill to Exclude results; Show me can do it for you.
